title: Maximum Size of a Set After Removals
statement: You get two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` that share the same even length `n`. Delete exactly `n / 2` elements from `nums1` and exactly `n / 2` elements from `nums2`, choosing which ones freely. Then put every element still left in either array into one set, where repeated values count only once. Return the largest size that set can reach.
notes:
## Intuition

Deleting `n / 2` elements from an array is the same as keeping `n / 2` of them, and keeping a value twice never helps, so each array really contributes up to `half` distinct values. A value found in only one array can only enter the set through that array, while a value present in both arrays can come from either. So each array should first spend its slots on its own exclusive values, and then the leftover slots of both arrays go to the shared values. Trying every pair of kept halves would also work but grows exponentially.

## Approach

1. Let `half = n / 2`, and build `set1` and `set2`, the distinct values of each array.
2. Count `common`, the values that appear in both sets.
3. `nums1` keeps `only1 = min(set1.size - common, half)` of its exclusive values; `nums2` keeps `only2` the same way.
4. Both arrays together have `2 * half - only1 - only2` slots left, and each one can hold a different shared value, so add `shared = min(common, those slots)`.
5. Return `only1 + only2 + shared`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums1 = [1, 2, 1, 2]`, `nums2 = [1, 1, 1, 1]`, so `half = 2`, `set1 = {1, 2}`, `set2 = {1}` and `common = 1` (the value 1). `only1 = min(1, 2) = 1` (the value 2) and `only2 = min(0, 2) = 0`. There are `4 - 1 - 0 = 3` free slots, so `shared = min(1, 3) = 1`. The answer is `1 + 0 + 1 = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): building the two sets and scanning one of them are linear.
- Space: O(n) for the two sets.

## Pitfalls

- Cap each exclusive count at `half`: an array with many distinct values still keeps only `half` elements.
- Leftover slots in one array cannot hold exclusive values of the other array; only shared values can fill them.
- Shared values are counted once in total, so cap `shared` by `common`, not by `2 * common`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `half` | how many elements each array keeps |
| `set1`, `set2` | the distinct values of `nums1` and `nums2` |
| `common` | number of values present in both arrays |
| `only1`, `only2` | exclusive values each array keeps |
| `shared` | common values placed in the remaining slots |

narration.2: Each array keeps exactly half of its elements.
narration.3: Collect the distinct values of nums1.
narration.4: Collect the distinct values of nums2.
narration.6: Walk over the distinct values of nums1.
narration.7: A value also in nums2 can be supplied by either array.
narration.8: Count it as a common value.
narration.11: nums1 keeps as many of its exclusive values as fit in its half.
narration.12: nums2 does the same with its exclusive values.
narration.13: The slots both arrays still have free can each hold a different common value.
narration.14: Exclusive values from both arrays plus the common ones give the largest set.
